# Two Sides of the Same Coin: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease and Atherosclerosis

**Authors:** Bo Zhu; Hao Wu; Kathryn S. Li; Shahram Eisa-Beygi; Bandana Singh; Diane R. Bielenberg; Wendong Huang; Hong Chen

**Affiliations:** 1.Vascular Biology Program, Boston Children’s Hospital, Department of Surgery, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 2.Department of Diabetes Complications and Metabolism, Arthur Riggs Diabetes and Metabolic Research Institute, Beckman Research Institute, City of Hope National Medical Center, Duarte, CA 91010

## Abstract

The prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and atherosclerosis remain high, which is primarily due to widespread adoption of a western diet and sedentary lifestyle. NAFLD, together with advanced forms of this disease such as non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and cirrhosis, are closely associated with atherosclerotic-cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). In this review, we discussed the association between NAFLD and atherosclerosis and expounded on the common molecular biomarkers underpinning the pathogenesis of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. Furthermore, we have summarized the mode of function and potential clinical utility of existing drugs in the context of these diseases.

## Abstract

## Introduction

The prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and its advanced form, the non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), have been surging globally [1]. In the United States alone, it is expected that by 2030, 100.9 million people will have been diagnosed with NAFLD [2], and approximate 25% NAFLD patients will have developed NASH [3]. A large number of NASH patients develop cirrhosis, necessitating liver transplantation [4]. Deaths due to liver failure are projected to increase by 178%, to an estimated 78,300 deaths in the United States in 2030 [2]. Unfortunately, a small portion of cirrhosis patients also develop hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [5]. NAFLD is the broad term that comprises isolated steatosis and hepatic steatohepatitis. The advanced NASH is strongly associated with fibrosis which can be evaluated using an established fibrosis score [6, 7]. Histological evaluation of liver biopsies still remains the only reliable standard for accurate diagnosis [8]. In addition to liver functional failure, the non-liver adverse outcomes of cirrhosis are also associated with increased risk of cardiovascular diseases [9], and type 2 diabetes mellitus [10]. Due to the metabolic component involved in disease pathogenesis, NAFLD has recently been proposed to be renamed as “metabolic associated fatty liver disease” or MAFLD [11].

Atherosclerosis is the major contributor to many cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), including coronary artery disease, stroke and peripheral vascular disease [12]. CVDs are the leading causes of death globally, and, according to the World Health Organization, there were 17.9 million CVDs-related deaths worldwide in 2019 [13]. In United States, approximately 610,000 heart deaths occur every year, accounting for 1 in every 4 deaths [12]. Atherosclerosis is a chronic disease that begins with the abnormal accumulation of lipids in the subendothelial layer of the arterial wall, followed by inflammation-induced atherosclerotic plaque progression [14]. Hence, the formation of fatty streaks is believed to be an anatomical hallmark of early atherosclerosis [14]. Atherosclerotic stenosis and atherosclerotic plaques emerge as a consequence of disease progression [15]. Strokes and myocardial infarction (MI) are the outcomes of atherosclerotic plaques in carotid and coronary arteries, respectively [16]. The atherosclerotic plaques can be classified as “unstable” versus “stable” plaques, depending on the thickness of fibrous cap [17]. Approximately two-thirds of stroke and MI cases occur due to unstable atherosclerotic plaque ruptures and thrombosis [18], and the degradation of thin fibrous plaques are mediated by abnormal accumulation of activated macrophages and foam cells [19].

Both NAFLD and atherosclerosis are classified as chronic inflammatory metabolic dysfunction diseases, and both are closely associated with defective lipid metabolism and inflammation (Fig. 1). In addition, both NAFLD and atherosclerosis are typified as having similar complications, such as obesity [20, 21], diabetes mellitus [22, 23], and dyslipidemia [24, 25]. Thus far, steady progress in understanding the underlying associations between NAFLD and atherosclerosis have been made [26, 27]. However, there have, hitherto, been limited studies addressing their common/shared mechanisms in a systematic way. This review focuses on the discussion of pathogenic associations between NAFLD and atherosclerosis and highlights the common potential biomarkers and therapeutic options for both NAFLD and atherosclerosis.

## Impact of NAFLD on the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis

NAFLD includes both nonalcoholic fatty liver (NAFL) and the more severe NASH. While NAFL presents with only isolated hepatic steatosis without inflammation, inflammation is an essential driver of NASH progression [28]. Both NAFL and NASH increase the risk of atherosclerosis (Fig. 2).

### Hepatic steatosis contributes to atherosclerosis

The liver is the central organ for the control of lipid homeostasis. The processes of de-novo lipogenesis (DNL) taking place in the liver and hepatic lipid metabolism are critical for regulation of the levels and distribution of lipids throughout the body [29]. Numerous studies have suggested that the dysfunctional hepatic lipid metabolism is highly associated to the onset of atherosclerosis [30].

Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is an important causal risk factor for atherosclerosis, and LDL receptor and Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) are required for clearance of LDL and triglycerides [31], and LDL receptor knockout mice and ApoE deficient mice are frequently used for the establishment of atherosclerotic mice models [32, 33]. Moreover, both LDLR deficient mice and ApoE knockout mice have been repurposed and successfully applied for the study of NAFLD [34, 35].

Hepatic sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP-1) overexpression in LDLR-deficient mice accelerates aortic atheroma formation through increase of the very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) cholesterol and reduction of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol [36]. In contrast, absence of SREBP-1 ameliorates atherosclerosis in mice lacking both SREBP-1 and LDLR [36]. In the liver, overexpression of SREBP-1 leads to hepatic steatosis due, in part, to the increase of lipogenesis [37].

Whereas peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) modulate lipid homeostasis [38], PPAR alpha regulates lipid metabolism in the liver, where it is highly expressed [39]. PPAR alpha participates in the pathogenesis of diet-induced atherosclerosis, and the concentration of atherogenic lipoproteins were higher in PPAR-α and ApoE double knockout mice than in ApoE knockout mice [40]. Mice with hepatocyte-specific loss of PPAR alpha developed hepatic steatosis [41].

There are other critical genes that are involved in the synthesis of hepatic cholesterol and triglycerides, including HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), the rate-limiting enzyme for de-novo cholesterol synthesis [42, 43], fatty acid synthase (FASN) [44, 45] and Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) [46, 47], all of which can serve as potential therapeutic targets for both diet-induced steatosis and atherosclerosis. Hence, emerging animal studies underscore that mediators of hepatic steatosis also contribute to the progression of atherosclerosis, suggesting shared pathogenic pathways.

Patients with steatosis have a high risk of developing subclinical atherosclerosis. A recently updated meta-analysis alludes to the association between NAFLD and subclinical atherosclerosis in Western and Asian cohorts [26]. NAFLD patients have a significant positive correlation with increased carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) and higher coronary artery calcification (CAC) score [26]. Consistently, at least one observational cohort study has found a positive correlation between NAFLD and subclinical coronary atherosclerosis [48]. Fatty liver diagnosis was confirmed via ultrasonography examination and coronary atherosclerosis was detected using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). This study reported that the ratios of atherosclerotic plaques were significantly higher in NAFLD patients, particularly, in NAFLD patients with a fatty liver index ≥30 with non-calcified plaque [48].

In addition, Colak et al. found that the mean Carotid intima media thickness (CIMT) was significantly higher in NAFLD patients than in control subjects [49]. Kim et al. also reported that NAFLD patients have greater CIMT than participants without NAFLD [50]. Huang et al. reported that NAFLD is associated with atherosclerosis in middle-aged and older participants [51]. The prevalence of NAFLD was observed in 30% of all participants, which was measured by ultrasonography. CIMT and brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (ba-PWV) had been measured, and remarkably higher CIMT and ba-PWV had been detected in subjects with NAFLD than those without NAFLD [51]. Another case study reported that NAFLD patients exhibited more carotid atherosclerosis than control subjects, with higher intima-media thickness (IMT) and higher preponderance of plaques than in the control group [52]. Bril et al. demonstrated that hepatic steatosis promoted atherogenic dyslipidemia in NAFLD patients [53]. Hence, emerging clinical studies support a strong association between NAFLD and atherosclerosis. These studies also compel us to infer that hepatic steatosis may contribute to the progression of atherosclerosis.

### Liver fibrosis promotes atherosclerosis progression

NASH is an advanced form of NAFLD, and is associated with hepatic fibrosis, hepatocyte injury, and death [6].Hepatocyte injury initiates inflammation by releasing cytokines and chemokines which further exacerbates hepatocyte injury [54]. Both resident Kupffer cells and monocyte-derived macrophages are involved in the release of proinflammatory chemokines and cytokines that further activate hepatic stellate cells, resulting in the formation of hepatic fibrosis [55].

Extensive studies have suggested that liver fibrosis is closely related to the progression of atherosclerosis [56]. It is well known that inflammation is an important causal risk factor for atherosclerosis [57], and it plays a central role in all phases of atherosclerosis [58]. Stable plaques can develop into vulnerable and ruptured plaques by thinning of the fibrous cap caused by inflammatory foam cells [58]. Many chemokines, cytokines and other inflammatory molecules have been reported to participate in both liver fibrosis and atherosclerosis. Both C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) and C-C motif chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) can promote hepatic fibrosis in mice by activation of hepatic stellate cells [59]. Consistently, significant reduction of hepatic fibrogenesis was observed in mice deficient for both CCR2 and CCR5 [59].

In parallel, atherosclerotic lesions were also significantly decreased in mice with a loss of both CCR2 and CCR5 [60]. In addition, other chemokines and cytokines partake in in both hepatic fibrosis and atherosclerotic lesion formation. For example, Interleukin-1 (IL-1) partakes in the progression of fibrogenesis by activation of HSCs [61], and IL-1 receptor deficient mice showed ameliorated liver damage and reduced fibrogenesis [61]. As expected, IL-1β also promotes atherosclerosis [62]. This is evidenced by the observation that IL-1β deficient mice exhibited decreased severity of atherosclerosis in an ApoE deficient and diet-induced atherosclerosis mouse model [63]. IL-6 also contributes to liver fibrogenesis [64], and, consistently, elevated IL6 levels contribute to the aggravation of atherosclerosis [65].

In addition, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) exerts pro-inflammatory roles that promote liver fibrosis [66]. TNFR1 knockout mice showed reduced liver damage and fibrosis [67]. Inhibition of TNFR1 expression significantly suppressed development of atherosclerosis [68]. Conversely, TNFα promotes the progression of atherosclerosis [69]. The extracellular matrix (ECM)-degrading enzymes, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and their inhibitors (TIMPs), are also reported to modulate liver fibrosis [70] and atherosclerosis [71]. Upregulation of TIMP-1 expression positively correlates to liver fibrosis [72] and calcification of atherosclerotic plaques [73]. MMPs activate hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and promote fibrogenesis [74], and MMPs are associated with the instability of atherosclerotic plaques [75]. On balance, there is converging evidence suggestive of a role for inflammatory chemokines and cytokines in both liver fibrogenesis and atherogenesis, indicative of shared common pathological pathways.

Emerging clinical evidence reveals that liver fibrosis increases the risk of atherosclerosis. A recent meta-analysis indicates the association between liver fibrosis and subclinical atherosclerosis [27], and the association is highly dependent on the degree of fibrosis [27]. In addition, a significant association was observed between the severity of fibrosis and maximum-CIMT (max-CIMT), and fibrosis scoring systems are instrumental in estimating the risk of atherosclerosis progression in NASH patients [56]. Similarly, participants with high NAFLD fibrosis score have a higher risk of developing subclinical carotid atherosclerosis [76].

Moreover, NASH-related cirrhosis patients have a significantly higher risk for developing atherosclerosis [77]. A retrospective study showed that liver cirrhosis patients have a higher risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) that lead to coronary stenosis [78]. Therefore, liver cirrhosis could be a risk factor for atherosclerosis. It was reported that cirrhosis patients had a markedly higher coronary artery calcification score than controls, and the total plaque volume, whether noncalcified or calcified, was higher in cirrhosis patients [79]. Liver stiffness is a critical indicator of fibrosis, and it can be measured by FibroScan, a non-invasive method to measure liver elasticity [80]. Following measurement of liver stiffness in NASH patients between the ages of 40–64, it was determined that liver stiffness > 4.5 kPa was highly associated with atherosclerosis, and that this was directly correlated with the burden of carotid and systemic atherosclerosis [81]. Therefore, according to clinical studies summarized above, we deduced that liver fibrosis and advanced cirrhosis are risk factors for development of atherosclerosis and atheroma progression.

## Atherosclerosis is a predictor of NAFLD

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease that also constitutes a major risk factor for cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). More specifically, atherosclerosis is a chronic, lipid and inflammation-driven disease of arterial intima [82]. As discussed above, many studies have reported that NAFLD can promote atherosclerosis. Further, atherosclerosis is not only one of the complications, but also a predictor of NAFLD.

### Atherosclerotic dyslipidemia and atherogenic index of plasma are predictors of NAFLD

The dysfunction of lipid absorption and transportation in the plasma, and the accompanying elevation in LDL cholesterol levels are directly associated with the onset of atherosclerosis [83]. Numerous clinical and experimental studies have demonstrated that aberrant plasma lipid accumulation, in particular, LDL cholesterol and triglyceride deposition, are closely related to the progression of hepatic steatosis [84]. Dyslipidemia is a lipoprotein disorder resulting in elevated LDL cholesterol and serum triglyceride levels, accompanied by decreased HDL cholesterol levels, promoting development of atherosclerosis [14]. The atherogenic dyslipidemia contributes to hepatic steatosis in NAFLD patients [53].

Liver-derived apolipoproteins and secreted plasma apolipoproteins are also involved in the pathogenesis of hepatic steatosis [85] and atherosclerosis [14]. It is reported that apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA-I) deficiency significantly promoted atherosclerosis in mice lacking LDL receptor [86]. ApoA-1-deficient mice showed increased diet-induced hepatic triglyceride deposition [87]. ApoA-4 deficiency is associated with atherosclerosis, and ApoA-4 expression restricts hepatic steatosis by inhibiting SREBP1-mediated lipogenesis [88]. ApoB lipoproteins act as the primary drivers of atherosclerosis [89], and inhibition of apolipoprotein B synthesis prevents steatosis [90]. In addition, ApoE deficiency results in a severe atherosclerosis [91], and promotes hepatic steatosis [92]. In summary, the experimental data discussed above indicates that apolipoproteins play critical roles in atherosclerotic dyslipidemia that could ameliorate symptoms of both atherosclerosis and hepatic steatosis.

Clinical studies suggest that atherosclerosis is strongly associated with NAFLD. Recently, Liu et al. reported that the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) was closely associated with NAFLD , and AIP is an NAFLD indicator that more accurate than other lipid parameters [93]. Furthermore, AIP is used as novel prognostic biomarker for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) [94]. Compared with the conventional parameters such plasma lipids, cholesterol, and triglycerides, the AIP showed a stronger correlation with the risk for NAFLD. Therefore, AIP could serve as a biomarker to screen NAFLD in high-risk individuals, in the hopes of reducing the prevalence of NAFLD. Consistently, using a systematic review and meta-analysis, Ismaiel et al. also reported that AIP is a reliable biomarker for diagnosis of NAFLD [95]. In agreement with this study, it has been demonstrated that AIP can be a useful predictor of NAFLD in obese adolescents [96]. AIP is also reported to be independent predictor for NAFLD in patients with type 2 diabetes [97]. Moreover, AIP is a novel predictor that can be used in the auxiliary diagnosis of NAFLD in obese participants [98].

Among non-obese participants, AIP was a strong and independent risk factor for evaluation of NAFLD, and screening for AIP in this population has been shown to be efficacious in prevention of disease progression to NAFLD [99]. In addition to AIP, soluble intercellular adhesion molecule (slCAM-1), plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1), and soluble CD40 ligand (sCD40L) are molecular mediators of atherosclerosis [100]. The circulating levels of sICAM-1, PAI-1, and sCD40L were markedly higher in NAFLD patients than in controls, with sICAM-1 being a strong indicator of histological severity in NAFLD patients [101]. In summary, elevated AIP, sICAM-1, PAI-1, and sCD40L can act as indicators of NAFLD.

### Arterial stiffness is an indicator of NAFLD progression

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease and inflammation plays a pivotal role in mediating all stages of this disease [57]. The plasma lipoprotein enrichment in the subendothelial space initiates the atherogenic process [102]. In the intima, LDL undergoes oxidative modifications by reactive oxygen species, and the oxidized LDL (oxLDL) is then taken up by macrophages for the formation of foam cells [103]. In parallel, oxidized phospholipids trigger inflammation of the arterial wall by binding to TLRs to activate proinflammatory signaling [104]. This is ensued by formation of cholesterol microcrystals by cholesterol loading that activate the inflammasome.

Cholesterol-laden foam cells trigger the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, as the inflammatory master cytokine, IL-1β activates the expression of many proinflammatory cytokines [102]. The infiltration of circulating macrophages, leukocytes, and monocytes into the atherosclerotic lesion pave the way for atherosclerosis progression [105]. Presently, the prevailing idea is that NAFLD can promote atherosclerosis given that liver is the central organ for LDLR synthesis that mediate the clearance of circulating LDL cholesterols. In addition, aortic atherosclerotic plaques may also contribute to NASH progression. Taylor et al. reported that the highly inflammatory aortic atherosclerotic lesion in cholesterol-fed rabbits may promote progression from NAFL into NASH [106]. In addition, Bieghs et al. demonstrated that NASH and atherosclerosis are two aspects of a shared disease, and activated macrophages play central roles in liver and atherosclerotic lesion genesis [107].The macrophage-induced systemic inflammation would further aggravate NASH and atherosclerosis progression.

Clinically, the carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cf-PWV) is recognized as a reliable parameter for assessing central aortic stiffness [108]. The increased arterial stiffness predicts cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, hallmarks of advanced stages of NAFLD [109]. Several studies have evaluated the correlation between NAFLD and arterial stiffness. Sunbul et al. evaluated 100 biopsy-proven NAFLD patients, in which those with NAFLD showed significantly higher aortic PWV compared to controls [110]. Ozturk et al. found significantly higher associations between NAFLD and stiffness in 61 biopsy-proven NAFLD patients, compared to 40 matched controls [111]. In addition, Chen et al. demonstrated an association between incidence of advanced fibrosis and subclinical atherosclerosis in 2550 participants with NAFLD [112]. In the above study, the extent of fibrosis was assessed using the NAFLD fibrosis score in NAFLD patients. For longitudinal studies, Li et al. evaluated the correlation between arterial stiffness and NAFLD among 1225 individuals in a five-year follow-up study [113]. This study concluded that NAFLD patients have a faster arterial stiffening than individuals without NAFLD [113]. Leite et al. performed serial cf-PWV measurements and liver fibrosis evaluation in a group consisting of 291 NAFLD patients over a seven-year follow-up study [114]. They concluded that increased aortic stiffness was associated with advanced liver fibrosis [114]. Therefore, NAFLD may promote arterial stiffness progression, and the increasing aortic stiffness may further drive NAFLD to advanced liver fibrosis [114].

## Shared molecular mechanisms underpinning both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Both NAFLD and atherosclerosis are chronic diseases that appear to arise from dysfunctional lipid metabolism, resulting in extra lipid / fatty acid accumulation in liver or blood, respectively. Both conditions are aggravated by excessive inflammation induced by the release of cytokines and chemokines. Both NAFLD and atherosclerosis share several common genetic risk factors, including polymorphisms of in specific alleles, microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and common NAFLD and atherosclerosis-associated genes.

### Genetic susceptibility to both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) suggest that polymorphisms in several NAFLD susceptibility genes, such as patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing 3 (PNPLA3), transmembrane 6 superfamily, member 2 (TM6SF2), glucokinase regulator (GCKR), membrane bound O-acyltransferase domain-containing 7 (MBOAT7) and hydroxysteroid 17β – dehydrogenase 13 (HSD17B13), promote the development of NAFLD [115]. The major variant and risk alleles of NAFL/NASH by GWAS analysis are highlighted in Table 1. Similarly, GWAS database, showing atherosclerosis-associated genes, suggests that SNP variants of ApoE and LDLR can lead to atherosclerosis. Other risk alleles for atherosclerosis have been highlighted in Table 1. Particularly, the ApoE−/− and LDLR−/− mice models can serve as valuable paradigms to study their shared contribution to both NAFLD [33] and atherosclerosis [32].

Aside from gene variants and genetic susceptibility, epigenetic mechanisms are additional modulators of gene expression, such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNAs. Non-coding RNAs consist of microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) that will be discussed in the context of the two diseases. Both miRNAs and lncRNAs may be involved in the pathogenesis of NAFLD and atherosclerosis. The common microRNAs and lncRNAs associated with both NAFLD and atherosclerosis are highlighted in Table 2.

### MicroRNAs and long non-coding RNAs commonly associated with both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that play crucial roles in the dysfunctional lipid metabolism and inflammation that are closely associated with NAFLD [116]. Therefore, the expression of specific microRNAs could serve as biomarkers of NAFLD. In addition, miRNAs play critical roles in cellular cholesterol homeostasis and the regulation of inflammation, both of which can drive the initiation and growth of an atherosclerotic plaque [117]. Many miRNAs can also be potential biomarkers for predicting atherosclerosis. We summarized the reported miRNAs that can be used as biomarkers of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis (Table.2).

Emerging evidence suggests that lncRNAs serve as critical regulators of hepatic lipogenesis and in mediating the expression of inflammatory cytokines in NAFLD/NASH [118]. In addition, lncRNAs play critical regulatory roles during the initiation, progression and resolution of atherosclerosis [119]. Therefore, these lncRNAs can be used as potential biomarkers of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. Similarly, in this review, we have summarized a list of lncRNAs that can be tested as biomarkers of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis (Table.2).

### Similar molecular clues underlying NAFLD and atherosclerosis pathogenesis

In addition to the non-coding RNAs discussed above, many coding genes/proteins are associated with NAFLD and atherosclerosis. We found NAFLD-associated genes (https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/Nonalcoholic+Fatty+Liver+Disease/CTD+Gene-Disease+Associations) and atherosclerosis-associated genes (https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/Atherosclerosis/CTD+GeneDisease+Associations) from the CTD Gene-Disease Associations Database that may serve as candidate biomarkers for NAFLD and atherosclerosis, respectively. We performed combined analysis of 2750 NAFLD-associated genes and 5445 atherosclerosis-associated genes and found that 1738 genes were overlapped between the two diseases (Fig.3A). Using gene ontology enrichment analysis, we found that lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and programmed cell death are the three major gene ontologies (GOs) that are associated with both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. We predict that the programmed cell death GO might be due to the widespread cell death in the atherosclerotic plaque and fibrosis-induced loss of hepatocytes. The GOs for lipid metabolism and inflammatory responses are directly associated with the common pathogenesis of NAFLD and atherosclerosis for dyslipidemia and inflammation. Therefore, NAFLD and atherosclerosis may be marked by shared signaling pathways driving their pathogenesis, some of which could potentially be used as common biomarkers for both conditions.

## Potential treatment for both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

### Non-pharmaco-therapeutic option: Dietary and lifestyle interventions to manage body weight

Consumption of “western diet”, typified by calorie-enriched foods consisting of high fat and carbohydrates, results in obesity and obesity is a strong risk factor for the development of fatty liver disease [20] and atherosclerosis [21]. For dietary lipids, the inflammation induced by polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) promote fibrosis formation in NAFLD [120] and plaque progression in atherosclerosis [121]. Over-consumption of carbohydrates significantly promotes the development of NAFLD [122] and atherosclerosis [123], especially highly lipogenic fructose [124].

Diet-induced obesity is highly associated with progression of NAFLD [20] and atherosclerosis [21]. Obese individuals who have a high body mass index (BMI) are at a high risk of developing NAFLD [125] and cardiovascular disease [126]. For advanced NASH, developing an effective clinical pharmacotherapy is urgently needed to solve the bottleneck of no FDA-approved medications. For mild NASH, the management of diet and lifestyle is the most effective approach to reverse hepatic fibrosis. NASH fibrosis regression can occur with 10% weight loss [127], and atherosclerotic lesion regression can be achieved after dietary intervention [128].

### Anti-dyslipidemia therapeutics for the treatment of NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Dyslipidemia contributes to the progression of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. Therefore, clinical drugs aimed at treatment of dyslipidemia may prove efficacious to ameliorate both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. The existing lipid-lowering drugs, with potential beneficial effects in both NAFLD and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease will be discussed.

#### Statins

Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) are the most widely used lipid lowering drugs thanks to their known efficacy and safety for the treatment of hypercholesterolemia [129]. In addition to its lipid lowering function, statins also play anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic roles that may be beneficial to anti-atherosclerosis [130]. A large body of evidence suggests that stains induce atherosclerotic plaque regression in a dose-dependent manner by reducing the level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol [131]. Statins have been shown to be safe and effective treatment options for NAFLD patients, and the utility of different statins for NAFLD and NASH have been evaluated by different studies [132, 133].

Simvastatin is an oral HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor that is used along with a proper diet to lower triglyceride and LDL levels [134]. In particular, it has been used for clinical treatment of NAFLD [135, 136], and has been shown to significantly reduce LDL cholesterol, with no significant improvement of hepatic fibrosis. Zhang et al. found with reduced blood lipid levels and decreased the quantity and size of plaques after simvastatin treatment in elderly patients [137].

Atorvastatin has been shown to significantly reduce hepatic steatosis in NAFLD patients and improve the metabolic parameters related to NASH [138, 139]. Peng et al. reported that atorvastatin can inhibit inflammatory responses, attenuating lipid deposition, and improving the stability of vulnerable atherosclerotic plaques [140]. Rallidis et al. showed evidence that pravastatin treated NASH patients showed improvement, based, at least, on histological assessment [141]. Chen et al. demonstrated that pravastatin mitigates atherosclerosis by inhibiting inflammatory macrophage accumulation in atherosclerotic lesions [142].

Pitavastatin has been shown to significantly reduce hepatic steatosis and fibrosis in NASH patients [143], and pitavastatin reduces inflammation within atherosclerotic lesions in chronic renal disease mice [144]. Mihaila et al. reported that lovastatin can decrease aminotransferase and cholesterol levels in NASH patients [145]. Frishinghelli et al. demonstrated that lovastatin slows progression or causes regression of atherosclerosis [146]. Kargiotis et al. reported an improvement of indicative parameters of NASH and its histological features in some patients after treatment with rosuvastatin [147]. Zhang et al. demonstrated that rosuvastatin exhibits anti-atherosclerotic effects by inhibition of foam cell formation [148].

Currently, statins are the safest and most effective pharmacological interventions for lowering lipid levels, which can target both NAFLD and atherosclerosis.

#### Non-statin lipid-lowering drugs

Fibrates or fibric acid derivatives are used for the clinical treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and primary hypercholsterolemia through the activation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR- α) [149]. Multiple studies have tested the safety and efficacy of these small molecules in treating hyperlipidemia in NAFLD/NASH patients and atherosclerosis [150]. Fenofibrate as a PPAR- α agonist has been widely used in the treatment of dyslipidemia [151]. Mice treated with fenofibrate have significantly improved hepatic steatosis and reduced fibrosis than control mice fed a high fat diet [152]. In a clinical study, Athyros et al. demonstrated the efficacy of fenofibrate in NAFLD patients, where 42% of NAFLD patients showed complete resolution of steatosis after 54 weeks of fenofibrate treatment (200 mg/day) [153]. In agreement with clinical studies, fenofibrate could significantly reduce atherosclerosis in mice and induce plaque regression in a rabbit model [154]. In a clinical setting, it was reported that fenofibrate treatment showed a significantly smaller increase in stenosis than the placebo control, in a study involving patients with type 2 diabetes [155].

Elafibranor, agonist of dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)- α and PPAR-δ , improves lipid metabolism and insulin sensitivity thanks to its anti-inflammatory roles [156]. In a double-blind trial, three groups were classified from 276 NASH patients : 1) 80mg/day elafibranor, 2) 120mg/day elafibranor, 3) or a placebo treatment for 52 weeks, and it showed that elafibranor (120 mg/day, for 52 weeks) resolved NASH without evidence for fibrosis worsening [156]. More notably, elafibranor also improved lipid parameters, such as lowering TG and LDL-cholesterol levels and raising HDL-cholesterol levels that might suppress the progression of atherosclerosis [156].

Niacin (nicotinic acid or vitamin B-3) has lipid-lowering effects, and it was shown to lower plasma levels of VLDL-triglycerides, without altering intrahepatic triglyceride content [157]. However, its safety and efficacy in NAFLD patients require further clinical studies. Su et al. reported that niacin suppressed progression of atherosclerosis and mitigated the levels of serum inflammatory cytokines in ApoE deficient mice [158].

Ezetimibe exerts its lipid-lowering effects by inhibiting the intestinal absorption of cholesterol [159]. Yoneda et al. reported ameliorated liver fibrotic lesion and mitigated hepatic lipids after 10 mg/day of ezetimibe for 6 months treatment in NASH patients with hyperlipidemia [160]. In addition, Ezetimibe prevents the moderate atherosclerotic lesion from exacerbation by mitigation of serum cholesterol, circulating inflammatory cytokines, and macrophage accumulation in the lesions [161].

The omega-3 (n-3) polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) decreases serum levels of triglycerides (TGs), Spadaro et al. reported that NAFLD patients who have received 2g polyunsaturated fatty acid per day for 6 months, showed significant improvement in serum AST, triglyceride levels and fatty liver [162]. In addition, Thies et al. demonstrated that the increase of n-3 PUFA intake can enhance the stability of atherosclerotic plaques [163].

LDLRs are the major receptors via which circulating LDLs are taken up, and PCSK9 promotes LDLR degradation and further results in higher levels of circulating LDL cholesterol. PCSK9 inhibitors were widely reported to be good candidates for lipid-lowering since they can prevent the degradation of LDLR by inhibition of the interaction between PCSK9 and LDLR [164]. Alirocumab releases more LDLRs to reduce circulating LDLs by inhibiting the binding between PCSK9 and LDLRs. Recently, Huang et al. reported that PCSK9 inhibition by alirocumab treatment ameliorates hyperlipidemia in biliary cirrhotic rats, however, it does not affect the intrahepatic inflammation and fibrosis [165]. In addition, a recent study demonstrated that treatment with alirocumab, in conjunction with high-intensity statin therapy, resulted in significant regression of coronary plaque burden and plaque stabilization on coronary computed tomographic angiography over 78 weeks in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia but without clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [166]. A recent in vivo CRISPR based-editing strategy, namely, VERV 101, achieved potent and durable inactivation of the expression of PCSK9 in the liver, resulting in significant reduction of LDL cholesterol in nonhuman primates, making it promising strategy to treat hyperlipidemia [167].

### Anti-inflammatory therapeutics for the treatment of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Although there are currently no FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of NASH, many compounds with related modes of function have been tested for resolution of NASH in preclinical tests. We will discuss the most promising drugs that have demonstrated positive preclinical outcomes in fibrosis resolution or regression.

Aramchol is an inhibitor of hepatic stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD1), and a recent clinical trial demonstrated NASH resolution without worsening fibrosis, in which 16.7% of those receiving Aramchol 600 mg, compared with 5% of the placebo group, exhibited NASH resolution [168]. In addition, Aramchol was reported to promote cholesterol efflux [169].

Aldafermin is an engineered analog of fibroblast growth factor 19, and the efficacy and safety of aldafermin have been investigated in a double-blind study of 78 patients with NASH at 9 research centers in the United States [170]. The Aldafermin group had higher percentages of significant reduction of liver fat content and fibrosis with no worsening compared to placebo group [170]. In addition, it was reported that Aldafermin had significantly reduced the 10-year ASCVD risk score compared with placebo [171].

Obeticholic acid (OCA), a farnesoid X receptor agonist, was also demonstrated to significantly improve fibrosis among NASH patients in a phase 3 study [172]. The Obeticholic acid 25 mg group has significant higher percentage of patients that with fibrosis improvement compared with the placebo group [172]. OCA may also be used to treat atherosclerosis by suppression of PCSK9 in human hepatocyte [173]. However, OCA may cause adverse effects in the progression of atherosclerosis due to reduced serum ApoAI and HDL cholesterol levels [173].

Seladelpar is a strong PPAR-δ agonist and, treatment with Seladelpar was resulted in robust reductions in markers associated with liver injury[174]. The reductions in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT), and alkaline phosphatase (AP) have been correlated with histological improvement in NASH [174]. In addition, treatment with Seladelpar resulted in significant improvements in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, all of which collectively suggest Seladelpar can improve atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases [175].

Resmetirom is a liver-directed agonist of thyroid hormone receptor-beta (THR- β) that for the treatment of NASH [176]. Harrison et al. observed that Resmetirom treatment for both 12 weeks (−32.9% Resmetirom vs −10.4% placebo) and 36 weeks (−37.3% Resmetirom vs −8.5% placebo) significantly reduce the hepatic fat in patients with NASH [176]. In addition, a recent phase 3 study of Resmetirom (MGL-3196) suggested that 1 year of treatment with Resmetirom was both safe and effective at lowering markers of both cardiovascular risk and NASH fibrosis, suggesting that Resmetirom can be a candidate drug for atherosclerosis[177].

Liraglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 analogue and has a significantly higher rate histological resolution (39%) than that of placebo (9%), and fewer NASH patients on liraglutide (9%) demonstrated progression of fibrosis compared to the placebo group (36%) [178]. At least one study reported that liraglutide may slow development of atherosclerosis and improve inflammatory status [179].

Lanifibrinor is a pan-PPAR agonist that modulates inflammation and fibrogenesis in NASH [180]. NASH patients receiving lanifibrinor had a significantly higher decrease of steatosis activity fibrosis (SAF) score than those receiving placebo [180] . Interestingly, although there are no experimental data supporting lanifibrinor-mediated amelioration of atherosclerosis, lanifibrinor was reported to significantly improve Adiponectin levels in patients with NASH [180].

Pioglitazone is a PPARγ agonist and treatment with pioglitazone was significantly associated with histological improvement in NASH patients [181]. Tian et al. reported that pioglitazone inhibits atherosclerotic plaque progression by controlling the Th17/Treg balance in atherosclerotic lesions [182].

Semaglutide, as a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, has been tested for its safety and efficacy in patients with NASH [183]. The phase 2 trial of semaglutide for the treatment of NASH patients resulted in a significantly higher percentage of NASH resolution compared in the placebo group [183]. Strong preclinical evidence supports that semaglutide confers substantial cardiovascular protective effects by inhibiting atherosclerosis [184].

It has been reported that fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) could serve as a potential therapeutic target for NASH resolution [185]. Efruxifermin, is a long-acting Fc-FGF21 fusion protein, and Efruxifermin treatment effectively reduced hepatic fat content in NASH patients [186]. In addition, efruxifermin was found to reduce circulating triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, effectively ameliorating dyslipidemia, which may reduce the risk of ASCVD in NASH patients. Pegozafermin is another FGF21 analogue and treatment with pegozafermin has recently been shown to significantly improve NASH resolution (compared with placebo), without aggravating fibrosis [187]. Intriguingly, pegozafermin treatment was also associated with reduced serum triglycerides in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia [188], hinting at the possibility that it may reduce the risk of ASCVD in patients with hypertriglyceridemia.

### Repurposing diabetes drugs to target NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Similar to obesity or diet-induced dyslipidemia, diabetes is a common complication of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. Therefore, drugs targeting diabetes could potentially be applicable for the treatment of NAFLD and atherosclerosis.

Metformin is the most common treatment for type 2 diabetes [189], and it has been applied for the treatment of both NAFLD and atherosclerosis. Evidence from several studies corroborate that metformin may mitigate both the onset and progression of NAFLD [190]. Metformin was also reported to suppress atherogenesis in hyperlipidemic mice via haematopoietic AMPK activation [191].

Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) are drugs that can increase insulin sensitivity. Two TZDs, namely, rosiglitazone, and pioglitazone, have been approved by the FDA for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus [192]. TZDs therapy was associated with improvement in advanced fibrosis and in NASH resolution [193]. TZDs were also shown to suppress plaque progression in diabetic patients with coronary atherosclerosis [194].

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1-RAs) have been approved for the treatment of obese T2DM patients thanks to their contribution to weight loss [195]. Growing evidence showed that GLP1-RAs reduce the degree of steatosis and improve liver fibrosis [196]. GLP1-RAs have also been reported to contribute to a reduction of atherosclerosis and reduced CVD by lowering plasma lipid and blood pressure levels [197].

Sodium-glucose co-transporter type-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i) are used for glucose control in T2DM patients thanks, in part, to their glucose-lowering function [198]. Several studies reported that hepatic fat was significantly reduced and liver fibrosis was significantly improved in type 2 diabetes patients with NAFLD following treatment with SGLT-2i [199]. In addition, SGLT-2i may be effective in suppressing atherosclerotic processes in patients with diabetes mellitus to reduce the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) [200].

### Identification of novel potential targets for both NAFLD and atherosclerosis

Having compared the atherosclerosis-associated genes with NAFLD-associated genes, we established that the overlapping genes are mainly enriched in gene ontology for: 1) apoptotic signaling pathways, 2) lipid metabolism, and 3) inflammatory responses (Fig. 3B). On this basis, we have discussed the potential applicability of drugs that target both lipid metabolism and inflammation. After enrichment analysis, we found the overlapped genes fall under the gene ontology terms for both non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis. Of the genes listed (Table.3), most of them have been identified as pharmacological targets for experimental studies to investigate their roles in atherosclerosis and NAFLD. In the near feature, potential targets to combat NAFLD and atherosclerotic disease are expected to emerge.

## Summary and Perspectives

There are several molecular, genetic and pathological parallels between NAFLD and atherosclerosis, suggesting the potential utility and relevance of common therapeutic strategies that could concurrently ameliorate pathogenesis of both diseases. In this review, we have endeavored to discuss the association between NAFLD and atherosclerosis, with an emphasis on illustrating their common pathogenesis, with a particular focus on dyslipidemia and inflammation. We have also expanded on several shared biomarkers in both diseases and the potential concurrent therapeutic strategies.

In the past decades, cardiovascular-associated mortality rates have steadily been increasing by virtue of a rapid rise in obesity and NAFLD incidence. Despite the high NAFLD/NASH prevalence, no FDA-approved drugs exist for the treatment of NASH. NASH is an independent risk factor for ASCVD, which is the leading cause of death in patients with NAFLD/NASH [201]. The link between NAFLD and cardiovascular disease has also been highlighted by the American Heart Association [202]. Identification of common biomarkers and candidate drugs for NASH and atherosclerosis will be instrumental in the reduction of NASH and ASCVD-associated mortality. In parallel, clinical trials seeking effective therapeutic interventions for NASH will be crucial to reduce the burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
